chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Business Cycle, Asset-Class Lens

lessons.title: The Four Phases: Expansion, Peak, Contraction, Trough

body.text: A business cycle has just four phases. Once you can place today's data in one of them, you know which asset classes have the wind behind them and which are fighting it.

children.text: The last lesson established that the business cycle drives asset returns through two dials, growth and inflation. This lesson slows down and looks at growth alone, broken into its four classic phases: expansion, peak, contraction, and trough. Get comfortable naming these, because every later chapter in this course, equities, bonds, gold, real estate, portfolio construction, is really asking one question: which of these four phases are we in right now?

markDefs.definition: The percentage of installed factory capacity actually being used to produce output. Tracked in India through the RBI's OBICUS survey. Low utilisation signals slack demand; utilisation near 80% or higher signals firms may need to invest in new capacity.

children.text: Economists have used this four-phase language for over a century, and it still holds up. An economy expands, growth accelerates then decelerates at a peak, contracts, then bottoms out at a trough before expanding again. The sequence never skips a phase, though the length and depth of each phase varies enormously from cycle to cycle. The clearest way to tell phases apart is to watch capacity
, hiring, credit growth, and corporate margins alongside the GDP number itself.

children.text: Peak Is a Turn, Not a Ceiling

A common mistake is to think "peak" means the fastest growth rate of the entire cycle. It usually does not. Growth is often still healthy at the peak, the defining feature is that the rate of growth has started decelerating from its high point. FY22's roughly 9% GDP growth, covered in the last lesson, was not a peak, it was a rebound off a crushed FY21 base. The real test of a peak is whether growth two or three quarters later is lower still, not whether this quarter's headline number looks impressive.

body.text: Because phases are confirmed by the trend across several quarters, you can only be fully sure you were at a peak or trough after the fact. This is not a flaw in the framework, it is exactly why markets, which price in expectations rather than wait for confirmation, tend to turn before the phase label is obvious to everyone.

body.text: India's FY21 trough was unusually sharp and short, one bad financial year, compared to how contractions typically play out. A large part of that was policy driven: lockdowns compressed years of demand destruction into weeks, and a strong policy and vaccination-led reopening compressed the recovery into a similarly short window.

body.text: Unlike the US, where the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) officially dates recessions and recoveries, India has no equivalent body issuing an official ruling on which phase the economy is in. The phase labels in this course are an analytical read of GDP, IIP, and other data, useful for building intuition, not an official verdict. Treat any phase call, including your own, as a working hypothesis you keep updating as fresh data arrives.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: IIP growth has been decelerating for three straight quarters after a strong run. Capacity utilisation is near 85%, but companies are still hiring and margins are still close to their cycle highs. Which phase best fits this description?
body.explanation: Growth is still positive and margins and hiring are still healthy, so this is not yet a contraction. The deceleration over three quarters, combined with near-full capacity utilisation, is the classic signature of a peak: still strong, but starting to turn.

body.label: IL&FS default
body.context: Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services defaulted on its debt, triggering an NBFC funding freeze that choked auto and real estate financing well before Covid hit.

body.title: Reading the IL&FS-to-Covid Stretch
body.scenario: In September 2018, IL&FS defaulted on its debt obligations, freezing funding across the NBFC sector that many auto and housing loans depended on. Indian passenger vehicle sales fell by double digits through 2019. Real GDP growth slid from roughly 6.5% in FY19 to about 3.9% in FY20, before Covid lockdowns arrived in March 2020 and pushed growth to roughly -6% in FY21.
body.prompt: Using the four-phase framework, how would you characterise FY19 through FY21, and what does this sequence teach about how confidently you can call a peak or a contraction in real time?
body.modelAnswer: FY19's still-healthy 6.5% growth was already past the true peak. The IL&FS default in September 2018 marked the start of a credit tightening that was only confirmed in the data a year later, when FY20 growth had roughly halved to about 3.9%, a clear contraction. That slow-motion contraction ran for close to eighteen months before Covid hit. What would likely have been a longer, gentler bottoming process was instead compressed into a sudden, deep trough within weeks by the lockdowns. The lesson: a peak is usually visible only in hindsight, after several quarters confirm the deceleration, and an external shock can turn what looks like a slow contraction into a much sharper trough than the pre-shock trend would have suggested.

cards.definition: Growth accelerating or holding above trend, capacity utilisation and hiring rising, credit expanding, margins improving.
Growth still positive but starting to decelerate, capacity near full use, early signs of tightening credit and cost pressure.
Growth slowing sharply or turning negative, hiring freezes or layoffs, credit demand falling, margins compressed.
Growth still weak but the pace of decline is decelerating, utilisation stabilising at low levels, first signs of policy easing taking hold.
The share of installed factory capacity actually in use, tracked in India via the RBI's OBICUS survey; a core coincident signal of where the cycle stands.

body.text: GDP, IIP, and event dates in this lesson are rounded, approximate, or drawn from widely reported figures, and are provided for education only. Phase labels applied to specific years reflect an analytical reading of the data, not an official determination, since no Indian body dates business cycle phases the way the NBER does in the US. Nothing here is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for advice on your own portfolio.

points: The business cycle has four recurring phases: expansion, peak, contraction, and trough, identified through GDP growth alongside capacity utilisation, hiring, credit, and margins
A peak is not the fastest growth rate of the cycle, it is the point where still-healthy growth starts to decelerate; a trough is not the deepest contraction, it is where the decline starts to slow
Because phases are confirmed only after several quarters of data, real-time phase calls are always provisional, which is part of why markets tend to move ahead of the confirmed data
Mapping India's FY19 to FY25 GDP numbers to phases shows a late expansion (FY19), contraction (FY20), a sharp trough (FY21), and a multi-year expansion since (FY22 to FY25)
India's FY21 trough was unusually sharp and short compared to typical contractions, largely because lockdowns and a strong reopening compressed both the fall and the recovery
India has no official body dating business cycle phases the way the NBER does in the US, so phase labels here are analytical judgment, not an official ruling
The IL&FS default in September 2018 shows how a peak or slow contraction can be identified only in hindsight, and how an external shock can compress a gradual slowdown into a sudden, sharp trough
